intro.title: Your first program
intro.bodyMarkdown:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web: every website you use runs it in your browser, to make pages react when you click, type and scroll. It runs on servers and in apps too. Your browser already has JavaScript built in, so in CodeQuest your code runs right here, with nothing to install.

A JavaScript program is a list of instructions that run from top to bottom, one line at a time. You type code into the sandbox or a challenge, press **Run** or **Check**, and the browser runs it.

Your first instruction is `console.log()`. Whatever you put inside the brackets is shown as output. Text goes in quotes, so JavaScript knows it is text and not code. Numbers and maths don't need quotes.

```
console.log("Hello, world!")
console.log(42)
console.log(2 + 3)
```

Each `console.log()` writes one line. The quotes make all the difference: `console.log("2 + 3")` shows the text `2 + 3`, while `console.log(2 + 3)` works out the sum and shows `5`. You can give `console.log` several things separated by commas, and it shows them with a space between: `console.log("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)` shows `2 + 3 = 5`.

Text can go in double quotes (`"Hi"`) or single quotes (`'Hi'`): both work, as long as the two ends match. CodeQuest mostly uses double quotes.

Lines that start with `//` are **comments**. JavaScript skips them; they are notes for the people who read the code. A comment can also go at the end of a line.

```
// Say hello
console.log("Hi!") // this line shows Hi!
```

Mistakes are normal, and JavaScript tells you about them. When it can't run your code, it stops and shows an **error**. `SyntaxError` means the code isn't written correctly, such as a missing bracket or quote. `ReferenceError: Console is not defined` means JavaScript doesn't know a name, usually because of a typo.

JavaScript is case-sensitive: `console.log` works, `Console.log` doesn't. Spelling matters exactly in the text you show too, because the challenges compare your output character by character.

You will often see lines that end with a semicolon, like `console.log("Hi");`. JavaScript adds them where they are missing, so they are optional here; CodeQuest leaves them out.
intro.sandboxCode:
console.log("Hello, world!")
console.log(42)
console.log(2 + 3)
console.log("2 + 3")
console.log("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)

challenges.title: Easy: Say hello
challenges.hint: Put the text in quotes inside the brackets: `console.log("...")`.

challenges.title: Easy: Two lines
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show `Ready` on one line and `Set` on the next.
challenges.hint: Each `console.log()` writes its own line, so you need a second one.

challenges.title: Medium: Let JavaScript do the maths
challenges.promptMarkdown: How many hours are in a year? Show the result of 365 days times 24 hours. Let JavaScript work it out: use `*` for multiplication.
challenges.hint: Put the calculation inside the brackets, without quotes: `console.log(365 * 24)`.

challenges.title: Medium: Text and maths together
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show `7 + 8 = 15`. Write the first part as text and let JavaScript calculate the `15`.
challenges.hint: Give `console.log` two things, separated by a comma: the text `"7 + 8 ="` and the sum `7 + 8`.

challenges.title: Medium: Fix the capital letter
challenges.promptMarkdown: This line fails. Run it, read the error, then fix it so it shows `Welcome`.
challenges.hint: JavaScript is case-sensitive. It is `console`, all lowercase.

challenges.title: Hard: Fix the quotes
challenges.promptMarkdown: This line has a `SyntaxError`. Fix it so it shows `JavaScript is fun`.
challenges.hint: Text needs a quote at both ends. One is missing before the closing bracket.

challenges.title: Hard: Comment it out
challenges.promptMarkdown: Turn the middle line into a comment, so only the other two lines are shown. Don't delete it.
challenges.starterCode:
console.log("Keep me")
console.log("Skip me")
console.log("Keep me too")
challenges.hint: Put `//` at the start of the middle line. JavaScript skips everything after `//`.

tests.label: Shows only the first and last lines
Keeps the middle line, as a comment

challenges.title: Expert: Seconds in a week
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show `Seconds in a week: 604800`. Let JavaScript calculate the number from 7 days, 24 hours, 60 minutes and 60 seconds.
challenges.hint: Multiply all four numbers: `7 * 24 * 60 * 60`. Give `console.log` the text and the calculation, separated by a comma.

tests.label: Lets JavaScript work out the number

challenges.title: Expert: Fix three mistakes
challenges.promptMarkdown: This shopping list has three mistakes. Fix them so it shows `Shopping list`, `Apples: 4`, `Total items: 7` and `Done`, one per line. Keep the sum: let JavaScript add `4 + 3`.
challenges.starterCode:
console.log("Shopping list")
Console.log("Apples:", 4)
console.log("Total items:", 4 + 3
consol.log("Done")
challenges.hint: Run it and fix one error at a time: a capital letter, a missing bracket, and a misspelled name.
challenges.solution:
console.log("Shopping list")
console.log("Apples:", 4)
console.log("Total items:", 4 + 3)
console.log("Done")

questions.explanation: Without quotes, JavaScript works out the sum first and shows the result.
In quotes it is text, so it is shown exactly as written, without the quotes.
It is `console.log`, all lowercase, with the text in quotes.

questions.prompt: What does JavaScript do with a line that starts with `//`?

choices.label: Skips it: it is a comment

questions.explanation: Comments are notes for people; JavaScript ignores them.
Several values are shown with a space between, and `4 + 4` is worked out first.
JavaScript is case-sensitive, so `Console` is a name it doesn't know.
A SyntaxError means the code isn't written in a way JavaScript can read, such as text without its closing quote.

questions.prompt: Which word comes before `.log` in the instruction that shows output?

choices.label: No: JavaScript adds them where they are missing
They turn the line into a comment

questions.explanation: Semicolons are optional in most code; JavaScript inserts them at line ends.
